# Open Science

## Open Science in the world

**The Open Science by UNESCO**

> Open science aims at making scientific knowledge openly available, accessible and reusable. The key elements of open science include: open access to scientific knowledge (including open access to scientific publications, data, educational resources, software and hardware); open infrastructures; open engagement with society and dialogue with indigenous and traditional knowledge systems, among others[^UNESCO].

[^UNESCO]: [UNESCO](https://www.unesco.org/en/open-science)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-unesco-logo.png){width=80%}
:::

::: {.column width=70%}

UNESCO asks member States to :

**1.** Promote a shared understanding of open science and set out diverse paths to achieving it<br>
**2.** Develop an enabling policy environment for open science<br>
**3.** Invest in infrastructure and activities that contribute to open science<br>
**4.** Invest in training, education, digital literacy and capacity-building to support open science<br>
**5.** Foster a culture of open science and align incentives to support it<br>
**6.** Promote innovative approaches for open science at all stages of the scientific process<br>
**7.** Encourage international and multi-stakeholder cooperation in the context of open science to reduce gaps in technology and knowledge<br>
:::

::::

## Open Science in Europe

**The Open Science by EOSC**

> The ambition of the European Open Science Cloud, known as EOSC, is to develop a ‘Web of FAIR Data and Services’ for science in Europe. The implementation of EOSC is based on a long-term process of alignment and coordination pursued by the Commission since 2015.[^EOSC].

[^EOSC]: [EOSC](https://eosc.eu/)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-eosc-logo.png){width=80%}
:::

::: {.column width=70%}

EOSC will also improve the situation for researchers in many ways, namely by :

**1.** Enhancing scientific research by providing access to a weath of data and research outputs from various fields and institutions.<br>
**2.** Fostering innovation by making it easier for researchers to share, collaborate and build on each others’ work.<br>
**3.** Improving transparency and reproducibility of research by making data and methods more open and accessible<br>
**4.** Reducing data silos and duplication of efforts by promoting data sharing and reuse<br>
**5.** Facilitating interdisciplinarity research and cross-sectoral collaboration by making data and resources from different domains more easily available<br>
:::

::::


## Open Science in France

**Second French Plan for Open Science**

> France is committed to ensuring that the results of scientific research are open to all, researchers, companies and citizens, without hindrance, without delay, without payment.[^french-plan]

[^french-plan]: [Second French Plan for Open Science](https://www.ouvrirlascience.fr/deuxieme-plan-national-pour-la-science-ouverte-pnso/)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .center width=40%}
![](images/logo-PNSO2.png){width=60%}
:::
::: {.column width=60%}
**1.** Generalize open access to publications<br>
**2.** Structure, share and open research data<br>
**3.** Open and promote source codes produced by research<br>
**4.** Transforming practices to make open science the default principle<br>
:::
::::

## Open Science in France

**The French Open Science Strategy (OSS) 2026–2033**

> The French Open Science Strategy (OSS) 2026–2033, aims to strengthen the transformations initiated with the two previous national plans. Covering eight years, it is structured around ambitions, challenges, strategic objectives, and four-year action plans. The 2026–2029 action plan breaks down 8 strategic objectives into 30 actions and 75 measures.[^OSS]

[^OSS]: [The French Open Science Strategy](https://www.ouvrirlascience.fr/french-open-science-strategy/)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .center width=20%}
![](images/image-OpenScienceStrategy.png){width=80%}
:::
::: {.column width=80%}
OSS Strategic objectives :

**1.**  Encourage a shift in practices to make open science the default approach<br>
**2.** Consolidate the governance and instruments of open science policy<br>
**3.** Reinforce the ecosystem of open science services and infrastructures, pillars of academic sovereignty<br>
**4.** Consolidate france’s position within the european and international open science landscape<br>
**5.** Structure and support open, reliable and high-quality academic publishing<br>
**6.** Consolidate the structuring of open and shared research data in accordance with the FAIR principles<br>
**7.** Increase the openness and valorisation of source code and software from research projects<br>
**8.** Ensure the transparency of clinical trials<br>
:::
::::

<!-- page 10 -->

## Definitions

#### **Data & Metadata**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=35%}

> Research **data** are defined as factual records in the form of figures, 
> texts, images and sounds which are used as the main sources for scientific 
> research and which the scientific community generally recognizes as being 
> necessary to validate research results[^oecd].
:::

::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image_DataMetadata.png){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width=35%}
> **Metadata**, which can be simply defined as **data about data**, is a way of 
> naming things and representing data and their relationships [...] Metadata is 
> structured information that describes, explains, locates, or otherwise makes 
> it easier to retrieve, use or manage an information resource[^borgman].
:::
::::
#### **Biodiversity data**

> **Artifacts** and **symbols** collected, stored, and disseminated in order to document the constituent elements of life, extant or extinct, at **any scale** of time and space. [...] These **elements are biological** and encompass anything that **contributes to the structure and function of life at any scale**, from the microscopic to the level of the planet, and to the **continuation of life, that is, its ability to persist and evolve over time**[^Garnier].

[^oecd]: [OECD (2007)](https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/science-and-technology/oecd-principles-and-guidelines-for-access-to-research-data-from-public-funding_9789264034020-en-fr)

[^borgman]: [Borgman (2020)](https://books.openedition.org/oep/14692)

[^Garnier]: [Garnier et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tree.2025.06.004)

## Data, datasets, databases and co

<br>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=45%}
![](images/data-circles3.png){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width=5%}
:::

::: {.column width=50%}

<br />


- **(a)** **Data** and **metadata** make up **(b)** **datasets**. 
- Multiple datasets in one location form a **(c)** **database**. 
- **(d)** **Aggregators** compile data from many databases. <br/><br/><br/>


- **Repackagers** transform data in a way that makes it more accessible for all audiences.
- **External users** (e.g. scientists, industries, government agencies etc.) access raw data by going through any or all of these data sharing portals.

:::

::::

<br />

::: {.citation}
**Source:** [Blair _et al._ (2020)](https://doi.org/10.3897/BDJ.8.e32765)
:::


## Relational databases


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=70%}

> A type of database that stores and provides access to data in tables that can 
> be linked to each through shared columns and rows, called **relations**, with 
> **unique identifiers** (keys) that show the different relationships between tables. 

<br/>

#### Codd's rules[^codd]: <br/>

1. Present the data to the user as relations (a presentation in tabular form, i.e. as a collection of tables with each table consisting of a set of rows and columns); <br/>
2. Provide relational operators to manipulate the data in tabular form. 

<br/>

**Tabular datasheets** used to be enough to store ecological data. Nowadays, 
with the increasing amount of biodiversity and environmental data, 
the use of **relational databases** is becoming much more frequent.

:::

::: {.column width=5%}
:::

::: {.column width=25%}
![](images/relational-database.png){width=100%}

:::

::::

[^codd]: [Date (2005)](https://archive.org/details/databaseindepthr0000date)

<!-- page 13 bis -->

## Characterizing data

<br/>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=40%}

![](images/image_DataMetadata.png){width=100%}

:::

::: {.column width=60%}

- **What** species?
  - Observation data: presence/absence, abundance, density, biomass?
  - What are the intra-population variations? DNA, trait measurements? Phylogeny?

- **Where** are they spatially? In which proportions?

- **When** were they observed or sampled? Repeated measures? Time stamp or global period?

- **How** were they collected? Biases? Pseudoreplication? True absences?

- **Why** and **Who**? Citizen science? Opportunistic? Funding? 

:::
::::

<!-- page 17 -->

## Data classification - By thematic and others

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=70%}

- **Longitudinal data**

Repeated measures, such as long term surveys, allowing to look at evolution (of abundances, biomass, etc) over time.

> Time series analyses

:::

::: {.column width=30%}

![](images/time-series.png){width=80%}

:::

::::

- **Spatial data**

Generic term that starts whenever there are spatial coordinates (long/lat) associated with an observation. May also refer to remote sensing images, GIS.

<br>

- **Textual data**

Again a very generic term, ranges from spreadsheets of data occurrences to DNA sequences, and text mining (systematic reviews, web scrapping, etc).


<!-- page 14 -->
## Data classification - Recap

<br/>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=33%}

**Format**[^eml]

- Data Table
- Spatial raster
- Spatial vector
- Databases
- Other entities
:::

::: {.column width=33%}

**Protocols and methods**[^kissling]

- Inventories (opportunist vs (semi-)protocole)
- Sensors
- DNA-based techniques
- Satellite remote sensing
- Others (simulated data)

:::

::: {.column width=33%}

**Thematic and/or other classifications**

- Temporal information (e.g. longitudinal data / time series (LTS))
- Spatial information (spatial data (GIS, occurrences, remote sensing, etc.)
- Textual data (csv, …)
- Taxonomic
- Trait data
- Non-exhaustive
:::

::::


[^eml]: [Ecological Metadata Language (EML)](https://eml.ecoinformatics.org/eml-schema)
[^kissling]: [Kissling *et al.* (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1111/brv.12359)

## CARE principles

#### **Definitions**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=70%}
>Indigenous data are data, information, and knowledge, in any format, that impact Indigenous Peoples, nations, and communities at the collective and individual levels; data about their resources and environments, data about them as Individuals, and data about them as collectives[^Carroll].<br>
:::
::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-logo-GIDA.png){width=100%}
:::
::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=70%}
>These principles, centered on Indigenous peoples, emphasize Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, and Ethics. They stress respect for the rights, sovereignty, and values ​​of Indigenous peoples regarding their data. They focus on protecting and respecting the individuals and communities from whom the data originates.[^DORANum].<br>
:::
::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-doranum-logo.png){width=100%}
:::
::::

[^Carroll]: [Carroll _et al._ (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-021-00892-0)
[^DORANum]: [DORANum (2023)](https://doi.org/10.13143/AF7S-G015)

<!-- page -->

## CARE principles

#### **The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=70%}
>The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) was adopted during the fifteenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP 15) [...] Among the Framework’s key elements are 4 goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030.<br>
:::
::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-logo-KMGBF.jpg){width=50%}
:::
::::

#### **Target 21** :Ensure That Knowledge Is Available and Accessible To Guide Biodiversity Action
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=70%}
>Ensure that the best available data, information and knowledge, are accessible to decision makers, practitioners and the public to guide effective and equitable governance, integrated and participatory management of biodiversity, and to strengthen communication, awareness-raising, education, monitoring, research and knowledge management and, also in this context, traditional knowledge, innovations, practices and technologies of indigenous peoples and local communities should only be accessed with their free, prior and informed consent[1], in accordance with national legislation[^CBD].<br>
:::
::: {.column .center width=30%}
![](images/image-target21.png){width=50%}
:::
::::

[^CBD]: [CBD (2023)](https://www.cbd.int/gbf/targets/21)

# Reproducibility concepts

<!-- page xxx @Nico -->

## What is reproducibility?

<br>

![Source: [https://eliocamp.github.io](https://eliocamp.github.io/reproducibility-with-r/materials/day1/01-introduction/)](images/reproducible-matrix.jpg){fig-align="center" width="50%"}


**Reproducibility** is about results that can be obtained by someone else (or you in the future) given the **same data** and the **same code**. This is a technical problem.

<br/>

{{< fa hand-point-right >}} &nbsp;We talk about **Computational reproducibility**


## What is reproducibility?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=50%}
![](images/image-Powers2018.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width=50%}
![](images/image-JenkinsReproductibility.png){width=100%}
:::

::::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=50%}
> Computational reproducibility frequently refers to the ability to generate 
> equivalent analytical outcomes from the same data set using the same code and software[^powers].
:::

::: {.column width=50%}
> [...] all raw data and metadata, code, programming scripts, and bespoke 
> software necessary for fully replicating any analyses that lead to inferences made in a published study[^jenkins].
:::

::::

[^powers]: [Powers & Hampton (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1002/eap.1822)
[^jenkins]: [Jenkins _et al._ (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.9961)



## Why does it matter?


> An **article** about computational results is advertising, not scholarship. The actual scholarship is the full **software environment**, **code** and **data**, that produced the result.

:::

<br/>

## Flux and stocks

**Sharing data and metadata from research activities requires making them available in repositories.**

It is recommended to prioritize deposits in **trusted thematic repositories** (eg. InDoRES, SEANOE, ...), or failing that in **institutional repositories** (eg. Data SUD, CIRAD Dataverse, ...), or failing that, in **generic repositories** such as [the Recherche Data Gouv repository](https://recherche.data.gouv.fr/fr/page/entrepot-recherche-data-gouv). Resources exist for choosing the adapted and recommended data repository.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .center width=33%}

![](images/image-selection-entrepot.jpg){width=70%}

[[Ouvrir la science (2024)]{.citation}](https://www.ouvrirlascience.fr/selectionner-un-entrepot-thematique-de-confiance-pour-le-depot-de-donnees-methodologie-et-analyse-de-loffre-existante/)
:::

::: {.column .center width=33%}
![](images/image-logigrammeFluxSI.png){width=90%}

[[Norvez *et al.*(2024)]{.citation}](https://mnhn.hal.science/mnhn-04296424/)
:::

::: {.column .center width=33%}
![](images/image-logigramme-rdg.jpg){width=58%}

[[Recherche Data Gouv (2024)]{.citation}](https://recherche.data.gouv.fr/fr/page/entrepot-recherche-data-gouv)

| [InDoRES](https://www.indores.fr/) | CNRS-Ecology, MNHN | Thematic & Institutional | Ecology, Environment, Bio-archaeology | Environmental, ecological and geographical data | Yes | DOI  |2 GB per data set  |
| [EaSy Data](https://www.easydata.earth/) | Data Terra, BRGM | Thematic | Earth and Environmental Sciences | Long tail data from the earth system and environment (example: project issues) | Yes<br/>(< 2 yr) | DOI  | 5 GB per file, 100 GB per deposit  |
| [SEANOE](https://www.seanoe.org/) | Ifremer | Thematic & Institutional | Oceanography | Georeferenced marine data | Yes<br/>(< 2 yr) | DOI  | 100 GB  |
| [Data SUD](https://dataverse.ird.fr/) | IRD | Institutional | All fields covered by IRD agents | ??? | ???  | DOI  | ???  |

## A complex landscape

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=40%}
<br/>

- Diversity of tools and practices (historical practices)
- Different supervisions
- Flow and storage of data and metadata
- Difficulty for data producers to identify the right information systems to deposit their data according to the scopes and themes
- Difficulty for users to know where and how to search for data
:::

::: {.column .center width=60%}
![](images/garnier-tee.png){width=70%}

[From [Garnier & Pavoine _et al._ (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tree.2025.06.004)]{.citation}
:::

::::




## A complex landscape

<br>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width=45%}
<br>
PatriNat wrote a document (in french) to support producers and reusers of biodiversity data and metadata in:

- Understanding the landscape (actors, who does what, who is who, etc.)
- Sharing (meta)data (where to deposit them, what types of data, etc.)
- Using the latter via information systems according to the themes and/or target audiences

<br/>

The targets of this document are mainly researchers, managers, engineers and data technicians
:::

## Take home message

- **Heterogeneity** (data types, origin, standards) & **diversity** of "objects" to be linked together[^1]
- **Loss of information** over time[^2]
- Toward a better **open science** and **reproducibility** [^3]^,^ [^4]
